headline: He built roads to end traffic. Traffic won.
dek: Robert Moses built 416 miles of parkway to get New York moving.

slides.label: The bright idea
slides.title: Jammed streets, too few parks
slides.text: New York needed parks, and its streets were jammed. A 1930 plan from a parks group Robert Moses chaired called for buying thousands of acres of the city's last natural land, plus parkways to fix the traffic.
slides.alt: Aerial view of cars streaming along the Grand Central Parkway through a looping interchange among houses and fields
slides.credit: Grand Central Parkway at the Kew Gardens Interchange, Queens, about 1946. U.S. Department of State. National Archives. Public domain.

slides.label: It worked
slides.title: Beaches, pools, playgrounds
slides.text: Jones Beach opened in 1929, and 350,000 people came in the first month. As parks commissioner from 1934 to 1960, Moses took New York from 119 playgrounds to 777 and opened 11 huge pools in the summer of 1936.
slides.alt: Aerial view of Jones Beach in 1936: wide sand, the boardwalk, bathhouses, the water tower and vast parking fields
slides.credit: Jones Beach from the air, 1936. U.S. Army. National Archives. Public domain.

slides.label: The backfire
slides.title: More road, more cars
slides.statLabel: people displaced for his highways alone, by biographer Robert Caro's count
slides.text: Caro found that the more highways were built to relieve congestion, the more cars poured in to fill them. Expressways like the Cross Bronx, built 1948 to 1972, cut through working-class neighborhoods.
also: Source: Robert Caro, The Power Broker, 1974
slides.alt: Traffic on the Cross Bronx Expressway in 1973, sunk below overpasses and ramps crowded with cars
slides.credit: Cross Bronx Expressway, 1973. Dan McCoy, EPA Documerica. National Archives. Public domain.

slides.label: Could anyone have seen it coming?
slides.title: Yes, and people said so
slides.text: In 1930 a transit executive told a St. Louis commission that widening streets simply produces more traffic. Caro documents Moses's own new parkways jamming soon after they opened, and Moses proposing about 200 more miles of road by 1942.

slides.label: The long cleanup
slides.title: Studying the damage
slides.text: In 2022 the federal government gave New York City $2 million to study how to ease the Cross Bronx's harm to nearby neighborhoods. In 2024 it added $150 million for a connector road with bus lanes and paths for bikes and walkers.

slides.label: The ledger
slides.title: Worth it?
gains: Playgrounds up from 119 to 777 in his 26 years as parks commissioner
City park land up from 14,000 to 34,673 acres
13 bridges and 416 miles of parkway, by one count
costs: 250,000 people displaced for his highways alone, by Robert Caro's count
Parkways that jammed soon after opening, as Caro documents
Bronx neighborhoods exposed to the Cross Bronx's noise and air pollution, officials say
slides.text: He gave a crowded city beaches, pools and parks. His roads moved cars well until more cars came, and some neighborhoods paid with their homes.

slides.label: Credit for trying
slides.title: We owe him one
slides.text: Moses took on real problems: a city that needed parks and streets choked with traffic. Jones Beach is still a state park. His roads also became a textbook case of what planners now call induced demand.

slides.label: Pattern
slides.title: Great for one, bad for all

slides.label: How the pattern works
slides.title: Faster for one, slower for all
slides.text: A new road makes the trip faster for each driver, so more people choose to drive, until it is slow again. A study of US cities found driving grows in step with highway miles and concluded more roads are unlikely to relieve congestion.

slides.label: How you do this
slides.title: Your shortcuts fill up too
slides.text: Every team marks its requests to engineering urgent so theirs get done first. It works for the first team, so the others follow. Soon every ticket is urgent, the label means nothing, and work ships no faster than before.
also: Every startup in a category bidding on the same ad keywords
Every feature asking for push notifications, until users turn them all off

slides.label: Lessons
slides.title: What we take from it
items: Making something easier tends to bring more of it.
Traffic is thousands of separate choices, and it responds to what gets built.
The people who pay for a road are often not the people who drive on it.

portrait.credit: Robert Moses with a Battery Bridge model, 1939. C.M. Stieglitz, World-Telegram. Library of Congress. Public domain.
